item.title: CISA Confirms PHP2Shell Exploitation, Orders Federal Agencies to Patch
item.description:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added two critical PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 26. The flaws were added after the agency received evidence that attackers have exploited the bugs.

PHP is a core programming language that runs nearly 70 percent of all web sites globally. According to estimates from Censys, over 32.5 million active PHP installations currently run vulnerable software versions.

The flaws are collectively called PHP2Shell and assigned a CVSS score of 9.2 each. CVE-2026-109618 involves memory corruption linked to out-of-memory handling, while CVE-2026-109619 involves stale internal request state. Both can let attackers run code remotely on vulnerable web servers without logging in.

The PHP team released fixes on October 21, but attackers have since managed to exploit the vulnerabilities. As Hackread.com reported the updates last week, these flaws affect several PHP configurations, including Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM and php-cgi. The PHP team specifically warned about mod_php, where a malicious request can trigger the flaw before the application processes it.

Successful Attack Reported

Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that attackers began targeting the flaws four days before the patches were released. Other security firms also detected exploitation attempts, although the early attempts they observed were unsuccessful.

That changed on October 24, when Adel Karimi, detection and response lead at Perplexity, reported successful remote code execution against a honeypot running Apache mod_php with PHP 8.4.26.

The response included an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, indicating memory disclosure during the exploit chain. The test demonstrated a working attack under that particular configuration, not that every vulnerable PHP server could be exploited in the same way.

Hackread.com also reported on NowSecure research that identified 426 Android and iOS apps connecting to servers advertising potentially affected PHP versions. The findings do not establish that all those apps were vulnerable, but they highlight the need to check the server-side software supporting mobile applications.

CISA’s Deadline and Fixes’ Details

CISA gave affected Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies until October 29 to address PHP2Shell. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

Those administrators using older versions should check with their hosting providers or software vendors for available fixes. Several vendors, including WordPress, Drupal, Craft CMS, Citrix, F5 and QNAP, have also issued advisories for products that may be affected.

The PHP team also disclosed a separate potential RCE flaw, CVE-2026-115560, on October 23, recommending that administrators disable session.upload_progress.enabled as a temporary mitigation.

Updated Windows builds released on October 26 also address CVE-2026-111497, a separate Brotli decompression flaw that can affect PHP’s cURL extension when automatic response decompression is enabled.

Expert’s Commentary

William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, shared his comments with Hackread.com, saying CISA’s confirmation backed up earlier concerns about the vulnerabilities.

“CISA has now confirmed the fears that were on everyone’s minds,” Wright said, noting that security vendors had previously detected attempts to exploit the flaws against honeypots and servers, although those attempts had reportedly failed to achieve remote code execution.

He warned that smaller websites and services could face greater risks if they remain unpatched.

“While major services were all promptly patched, the question remains about what will happen to smaller, unmaintained sites and services, and to the many instances where PHP is hidden as part of a tech stack supporting services like internal organization portals and CMS’.”

Wright urged organisations to check their own infrastructure as well as systems managed by external providers and partners.

“Organizations need to review their systems ASAP and ensure that they are not silently exposed to unpatched PHP deployments, whether internally or via third parties and partners.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience…

item.title: Sweet Security Offers All Organizations Affected by HTTP2Shell Virtual Patching Protection at No Cost
item.description:
New York, NY, October 27th, 2026, CyberNewswire

The root-cause fix will take weeks; protection can’t wait

Sweet Security today announced Sweet Safety Net, extending its runtime Virtual Patching protection to every organization affected by HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497). The capability will enable users to block any exploitation of Node2Shell at no cost for 30 days, whether or not they are Sweet customers. 

HTTP2Shell sits inside the Brotli decoder built into Node.js, Bun, Python, Envoy, Istio and, as Sweet’s own research revealed this week, Go frameworks such as Traefik, Fiber and Iris. Patching it everywhere will take weeks. Sweet Safety Net gives affected teams protection at the vulnerable code path, with no code changes, no commitment, while engineering ships the permanent fix.

Sweet Security is already observing active exploitation attempts across 88% of monitored environments. 

“We are watching HTTP2Shell exploitation attempts in real environments right now,” said Dror Kashti, CEO and co-founder of Sweet Security. “We’re extending our protection to organizations that need help securing affected applications. Sweet Safety Net exists because every organization deserves the same visibility and protection our customers have – especially in a moment like this. Virtual Patching closes the exploitation path today. The permanent fix can follow.”

The Root-Cause Fix Will Take Weeks. Protection Can’t Wait.

HTTP2Shell lives in the Brotli decoder compiled into the runtimes and libraries that applications are built on. Fixing it at the root means updating every affected dependency, rebuilding applications that bundle the decoder, testing the changes and redeploying them across production. For most organizations, that will take weeks. For the whole time, the vulnerable code keeps running and stays reachable by attackers.

Sweet’s Virtual Patching closes that gap with a surgical fix at runtime. Instead of waiting for the code to change, Sweet stops the attack payload before it reaches the vulnerable code path, and legitimate traffic keeps flowing. The bug is still in the code, but it can no longer be exploited. 

Teams get protection now and can ship the permanent fix on their own timeline, without the pressure of an open exposure. 

What Virtual Patching Does

Sweet Security’s Virtual Patching protects running applications while engineering completes the permanent fix. Sweet applies a protection policy through its sensor, targeting the vulnerable code path and blocking exploitation while legitimate traffic continues. No application code change is required. Teams apply the policy from Sweet’s Vulnerabilities Catalog, and Sweet distributes it to sensors on each node running the affected workload. Once the sensors confirm enforcement, the workload is marked Protected from that vulnerability. Protection follows the workload as it scales and restarts.

Sweet customers can use the Vulnerabilities Catalog to apply protection to affected workloads and confirm enforcement through the Protected status.

Sweet Security customers are already protected. Sweet’s runtime sensors and L7 detection rules are active across all customer tenants, with exploitation attempts already detected and blocked in monitored environments.

The Sweet Safety Net

Effective immediately, any organization can claim Sweet Security sensors with Virtual Patching protection for 30 days. No purchase commitment is required.

To claim the offer, please visit: https://hi.sweet.security/http2shell-virtual-patching-sweet-safety-net#activate 

About Sweet Security

Sweet Security delivers a proactive runtime security platform for cloud and AI. By understanding how applications, identities, and AI agents behave in live environments, Sweet helps security teams discover what’s running, prove which weaknesses attackers can exploit before it happens, harden their defenses, and stop malicious activity in real time. Trusted by the world’s leading AI companies to secure the next frontier, Sweet gives organizations the visibility and control to adopt new technologies with confidence while protecting the systems their businesses depend on.

item.title: Fake US Court Notices Target 100,000+ Businesses With LodaRAT
item.description:
Fake US court notices target over 100,000 businesses, luring recipients to download LodaRAT malware that steals passwords, records activity and controls PCs.

Cybersecurity researchers at ThreatDown have uncovered a large-scale phishing campaign impersonating the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida. The operation has so far targeted more than 100,000 businesses using fake notices regarding Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) cases to trick recipients into downloading malware.

The emails contain unique civil case identifiers and links to a fraudulent court portal that displays each target company’s name and contact details. To evade security filters, the site restricts access based on the visitor’s browser software, displaying content only to users who visit using Microsoft Edge.

The US District Court for the Southern District of Florida has issued an official alert to warn the public about these fraudulent communications.

Three Routes Deliver the Same Malware

Once on the site, targets are urged to download a password-protected compressed file to view their case documentation. The file contains a single optical disk image (ISO) containing three different file types: an MSC file, a batch file and a Windows shortcut. Opening any of the files triggers a distinct execution path, though all three routes ultimately download the same malware.

The payloads come from a typosquatted domain, us.wind0ws.net, and use filenames associated with legitimate Windows components: Taskmgr.exe, SystemSettings.exe and msedge.exe.

ThreatDown identified the malware as LodaRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) that allows attackers to remotely control infected systems. Hackread.com previously reported on LodaRAT in 2021, when researchers documented a version capable of targeting Android devices.

ThreatDown found that LodaRAT contains extensive surveillance mechanisms. It can capture keystrokes, steals saved login credentials from major web browsers, records audio and video, and extracts Wi-Fi passwords. It can also enable Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) connections and spread across local networks.

How LodaRAT Maintains Access

LodaRAT sets up registry Run keys, startup shortcuts and scheduled tasks to launch again after a reboot, and drops a VBScript watchdog that checks whether the malware is running. It starts it again if the process is stopped.

Researchers traced the campaign’s infrastructure to courtadr.com, a roughly 20-year-old domain. They observed changes to its certificate management beginning in March 2026, followed by the creation of supporting subdomains. However, the available evidence does not establish whether the original domain was compromised.

“Threat actors are now investing heavily in the front end of attacks (compromised domains, credible branding, personalized targeting) precisely because the back end (commodity malware) remains so cheap and effective,” the researchers explained in the blog post shared with Hackread.com.

The findings highlight how personalized legal-themed emails can be used to deliver malware while making fraudulent requests appear credible.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Fake AI Attacks Target US Firms as Researchers Warn of Corporate Credential Theft
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was provided by ANY.RUN. The information and analysis presented are based on their research and findings.

An employee downloads an AI application or follows a seemingly legitimate setup guide. Everything looks normal, but behind the scenes, attackers may be stealing corporate credentials, hijacking browser sessions, or gaining access to business systems.

New research from ANY.RUN, based on 1,258 public sandbox analyses, reveals how attackers exploit trusted AI brands and legitimate platforms to target organizations, including those in the US. The findings raise a critical question for security leaders: Can existing security controls detect these threats before corporate access is compromised?

US Companies Among the Main Targets of Fake AI Campaigns

Between April and October 2026, ANY.RUN researchers examined 1,258 public sandbox analyses linked to fake AI campaigns. Among submissions with available country information, the US accounted for 16%, second only to India.

The US also ranked first in two specific attack categories: fake Claude download campaigns and ChatGPT-themed attack chains.

The research shows that attackers are using more than counterfeit download pages. Malicious installation instructions, shared AI conversations, and advertising campaigns are creating multiple opportunities to reach employees and compromise business accounts.

How Fake AI Attacks Unfold

Although attackers impersonate different AI brands, many campaigns follow a similar pattern. Employees encounter what appears to be a legitimate AI service, follow installation instructions, and unknowingly execute malicious code.

A typical attack involves four stages:

  • Initial contact: Attackers reach employees through fake ChatGPT or Claude websites, sponsored search results, or shared AI conversations.
  • Employee interaction: The victim downloads an installer or follows instructions to run a command in PowerShell or Terminal.
  • Malware execution: Malicious code runs in the background, potentially deploying infostealers or collecting browser credentials and session data.
  • Corporate exposure: Stolen credentials or active sessions may allow attackers to access business accounts and sensitive information.

In one case investigated by ANY.RUN, a trojanized Claude installer launched the real application while secretly creating a scheduled task to collect browser session data. The application appeared to work normally, even though malicious activity was taking place in the background.

What Fake AI Attacks Put at Risk for US Businesses

A single malicious AI download can create problems far beyond one compromised device. When attackers steal credentials, hijack browser sessions, or gain remote access, the consequences can spread across business operations.

The main risks include:

  • Compromised corporate accounts: Stolen credentials and browser sessions may give attackers access to business email, cloud services, and internal applications.
  • Exposure of sensitive information: Unauthorized access can put customer data, financial records, and confidential business documents at risk.
  • Broader network compromise: Malware deployed through fake AI installers can provide a foothold for further malicious activity across corporate systems.
  • Operational disruption: Investigating compromised accounts and endpoints can require device isolation, session revocation, and temporary restrictions on business applications.

For security leaders, these risks extend beyond malware prevention. They affect business continuity, data security, and the resources required to investigate and recover from an incident.

How Enterprises Can Detect and Respond to Fake AI Attacks

For enterprises, addressing these risks requires more than blocking suspicious downloads. Security teams need reliable ways to examine unknown files, investigate malicious behavior, and identify threats across their existing infrastructure.

Three capabilities can help organizations strengthen their response:

  • Analyze suspicious files and links in an isolated environment: ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox lets analysts safely examine AI installers, URLs, and scripts to uncover hidden processes, malicious network connections, and credential-stealing activity. In a separate enterprise study, one financial organization achieved a median threat detection time of just 15.1 seconds during sandbox investigations.
  • Give analysts the evidence needed to respond: ANY.RUN’s Tier-1 Reports provide structured investigation findings, including threat verdicts, observed behavior, and recommended next steps. This helps teams reduce manual analysis and make better-informed escalation and containment decisions.
  • Identify known threats across the security stack: ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Feeds deliver continuously updated malicious indicators to existing SIEM, EDR, and SOAR systems, helping teams detect known malicious infrastructure within their established workflows.

Together, these capabilities give SOC teams the visibility and investigation context needed to make informed response decisions without adding unnecessary manual work.

Limit the Damage of Fake AI Attacks with Faster Response

As fake AI campaigns exploit everyday business workflows, enterprises need security operations that can keep pace without increasing analyst workload or investigation costs.

Organizations using ANY.RUN report 20% less time spent on Tier-1 investigations, 30% fewer escalations to Tier-2, and 21 minutes less MTTR per incident. These improvements help security teams manage growing threat volumes with existing resources while reducing the potential impact of security incidents.

item.title: Scanner Poses as 32 AI Bots to Find Credentials and Private Keys
item.description:
A threat actor is impersonating roughly 32 artificial intelligence (AI) bots to scan websites for exposed credentials and sensitive configuration files, according to research from cybersecurity firm Cequence Security.

Cequence Security researcher Will Glazier tracked the scanner from late September through late October 2026 as it posed as crawlers and assistants associated with OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta and other companies.

On a single day in October, it reached 48% of the organizations monitored by Cequence that received AI bot traffic. The affected organizations spanned financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy and software. Nearly all requests from the scanner were blocked or failed during the observation period.

How the Scanner Operates

The scanner rotates through different bot identities, sometimes claiming to represent OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity within seconds of one another. It requests files that legitimate crawlers have no reason to access, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files and private SSH keys. The research identified a list of about 90 paths targeted by the scanner.

The activity also makes blocking individual IP addresses difficult. The scanner used more than 300 cloud IP addresses in one day and nearly 400 in a week. None of the addresses observed in late September reappeared a month later.

Each address sends between 50 and 190 requests in about eight seconds before the scanner moves to another address. It also sends random, nonsensical URL paths to identify websites that respond to arbitrary requests.

Why Banks Should Be Concerned

The findings come as banks and other businesses work out how to handle legitimate AI agents acting on customers’ behalf. Yet these agents still account for a small share of traffic at financial institutions. Even at the most exposed bank in the study, customer-facing agents represented about one in every 4,000 requests. Most AI-related traffic at banks came from crawlers collecting publicly available pages.

Because organizations often grant permissions based on self-reported agent names, attackers are easily exploiting those unverified labels to bypass standard perimeter security.

Cequence Security recommends that companies avoid trusting a bot’s self-reported identity alone. Organizations should verify incoming traffic through cryptographic request signing, verified address ranges, direct integrations, and behavioral analysis.

The findings follow similar research from Fastly, which reported on October 13 that it had recorded about 6.3 million requests impersonating AI crawlers and fetchers in 24 hours. The requests came from nearly 10,200 IP addresses and targeted .env files, Git metadata and other sensitive files.

Fastly’s findings point to the same concern raised by Cequence: attackers are using trusted AI bot identities to search for exposed secrets. The two investigations examined separate traffic samples.

The findings raise questions about how organizations verify automated traffic and manage access for AI agents. Patrick Harr, CEO of DataVisor, warned that attackers can change their techniques faster than traditional defences can adapt.

“Fraud is now polymorphic: AI lets attackers vary their approach every time, so legacy, static fraud defenses decay faster than teams can update them,” Harr told Hackread.com. “Institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers do. The same technology that creates the exposure can help close it.”

A threat actor is impersonating roughly 32 artificial intelligence (AI) bots to scan websites for exposed credentials and sensitive configuration files, according to research from cybersecurity firm Cequence Security.

Cequence Security researcher Will Glazier tracked the scanner from late September through late October 2026 as it posed as crawlers and assistants associated with OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta and other companies.

On a single day in October, it reached 48% of the organizations monitored by Cequence that received AI bot traffic. The affected organizations spanned financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy and software. Nearly all requests from the scanner were blocked or failed during the observation period.

How the Scanner Operates

The scanner rotates through different bot identities, sometimes claiming to represent OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity within seconds of one another. It requests files that legitimate crawlers have no reason to access, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files and private SSH keys. The research identified a list of about 90 paths targeted by the scanner.

The activity also makes blocking individual IP addresses difficult. The scanner used more than 300 cloud IP addresses in one day and nearly 400 in a week. None of the addresses observed in late September reappeared a month later.

Each address sends between 50 and 190 requests in about eight seconds before the scanner moves to another address. It also sends random, nonsensical URL paths to identify websites that respond to arbitrary requests.

Why Banks Should Be Concerned

The findings come as banks and other businesses work out how to handle legitimate AI agents acting on customers’ behalf. Yet these agents still account for a small share of traffic at financial institutions. Even at the most exposed bank in the study, customer-facing agents represented about one in every 4,000 requests. Most AI-related traffic at banks came from crawlers collecting publicly available pages.

Because organizations often grant permissions based on self-reported agent names, attackers are easily exploiting those unverified labels to bypass standard perimeter security.

Cequence Security recommends that companies avoid trusting a bot’s self-reported identity alone. Organizations should verify incoming traffic through cryptographic request signing, verified address ranges, direct integrations, and behavioral analysis.

The findings follow similar research from Fastly, which reported on October 13 that it had recorded about 6.3 million requests impersonating AI crawlers and fetchers in 24 hours. The requests came from nearly 10,200 IP addresses and targeted .env files, Git metadata and other sensitive files.

Fastly’s findings point to the same concern raised by Cequence: attackers are using trusted AI bot identities to search for exposed secrets. The two investigations examined separate traffic samples.

The findings raise questions about how organizations verify automated traffic and manage access for AI agents. Patrick Harr, CEO of DataVisor, warned that attackers can change their techniques faster than traditional defences can adapt.

“Fraud is now polymorphic: AI lets attackers vary their approach every time, so legacy, static fraud defenses decay faster than teams can update them,” Harr told Hackread.com. “Institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers do. The same technology that creates the exposure can help close it.”

item.title: OffSec Launches Free PHP2Shell Lab Following Critical Vulnerability Discovery
item.description:
New York, United States, October 28th, 2026, CyberNewswire

New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery.

OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) firsthand. Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations.

The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. 

They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress.

PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. 

Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. 

“PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec. “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.”

OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB. 

AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation

PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. 

“At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. 

“LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.”

The Effects of These Flaws

Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error.

“PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.”

That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges.

The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. 

The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here.

OffSec’s Current Recommendations

These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations.

  • Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone.
  • Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect.
  • Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching.
  • Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate.

Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense.

When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond. 

OffSec’s PHP2Shell lab helps practitioners turn technical knowledge into hands-on experience they can apply to future vulnerabilities. For a deeper look at the vulnerabilities, explore OffSec’s technical analysis. Organizations looking to build these capabilities across their security teams can explore OffSec’s workforce development programs.

About OffSec

OffSec is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

item.title: Summit Public Schools Breach Exposes 115 GB of Student and Staff Data
item.description:
A hacker has leaked 115 GB of Summit Public Schools data containing billions of lines, student and staff personal records and approximately 21,000 email addresses.

Names, home addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, parents details and school records of thousands of students and teachers are among the 115 GB of Summit Public Schools data published on a hacking forum.

Hackread.com examined the collection and verified that it contains personal information associated with the school network, including historical records and student account fields.

The files appeared on PwnForums on October 22, 2026, posted by an account using the name Sp1d3yG0nz4l3s. The account claimed to have breached the organisation’s cloud environment and described the release as approximately 100 GB, saying it was part of a larger collection. Hackread.com’s review puts the available files at 115 GB and identified approximately 21,000 email addresses.

Summit Public Schools operates schools in California and Washington. Although the forum post introduces Summit Tamalpais, one campus within the network, the released files include California and Washington school exports, education-service records and alumni information.

Personal Information and Historical School Records Exposed

Records examined by Hackread.com contain full names, dates of birth, residential and mailing addresses, gender, ethnicity, student identification numbers and enrollment information.

Some entries also include graduation years, transfer comments and administrative records. Student account usernames and populated password fields also appear in the collection. The reviewed password values are not readable plaintext, and their format and current usability remain unclear.

The files also contain older information, including enrollment entries from 2018 and 2019 and transaction timestamps from 2021. Separate person records list internal identifiers, active-status flags, creation and modification dates and the names of people who last changed entries.

Taken together, the files contain billions of lines, according to Hackread.com’s analysis. That total includes repeated entries that have not been removed, so it cannot be used as a count of individual records or affected people. The approximately 21,000 email addresses likewise should not be read as a victim total.

However, with names, birth dates and addresses available together, criminals could use the information to impersonate school employees or send convincing messages to students, parents and former students.

PowerSchool, Clever and Salesforce Exports Included

The collection is divided into folders labelled POWERSCHOOL_CA, POWERSCHOOL_WA, CLEVER and SALESFORCE_SUMMITPSALUMNI.

Within the California PowerSchool folder, TEACHERS.csv and USERS.csv are listed at 15.82 GB and 8.06 GB. The Washington folder contains six exports covering students, teachers, users, people, email addresses and telephone numbers.

Its largest file, STUDENTS.csv, is 35.12 GB, followed by PERSON.csv at 13.89 GB, while student and teacher exports in the Clever directory are organised under six education-service names, including:

  1. Khan Academy
  2. Lexia Core5 PowerUp
  3. MyLexia
  4. Newsela
  5. NWEA
  6. ST Math

The files also include alumni account and contact records in a Salesforce folder, with the two exports measuring 46.90 MB and 92.68 MB. The hacker used Salesforce and Snowflake hashtags in the forum post but did not explain how either platform was involved. No separate Snowflake folder appears in the listing.

Previously, ShinyHunters hackers breached the Salesforce environment of Instructure, the company behind the Canvas learning management system used by schools and universities worldwide, through social engineering in September 2025.

A separate Canvas breach in May 2026 involved its Free-for-Teacher environment, not a Salesforce flaw. No connection between those incidents and the Summit release has been identified. bitdefender.com

Hacker Claims Access Through a Critical Vulnerability

According to the forum account, an unspecified critical vulnerability allowed access to Summit’s cloud environment in October.

The poster said the weakness was patched an hour after the organisation was contacted, but supplied no CVE identifier, supporting correspondence or technical explanation.

Many files carry October 22 timestamps, although the collection includes information dating back several years. The date of the forum release therefore does not identify when the records were taken.

Claims of Student Medical Data Remain Unverified

The account also claimed to possess students’ medical conditions, descriptions of those conditions and assigned doctors. Records reviewed by Hackread.com contain medical-alert and doctor-contact fields, but the examined medical-alert entries were empty. One doctor entry contained an uncertain response and an apparently placeholder telephone number. Genuine diagnoses or doctors’ contact details have not been verified.

Nevertheless, the published material leaves students, families and employees facing exposure of personal information while the affected campuses and number of individuals remain unresolved.

Anyone receiving messages referring to these records should verify requests directly with their school, particularly requests for passwords, payments or additional personal details.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: From Rules to AI and Back
item.description:
This article discusses the evolution of fraud prevention techniques. Fraud-prevention systems have to balance several competing demands: catching fraudulent activity without blocking legitimate customers, adapting quickly to new attack patterns, processing decisions efficiently and keeping those decisions explainable.

It covers the period from the 1970s to the present, when companies moved from rules-based approaches to relying on ML and then eventually adopted hybrid approaches. We’ll look into the main driving forces that caused each shift, the problems each new approach tried to solve and who was first to make the move.

Rules-Based Era

In 1973, Visa launched VisaNet that brought computerised authorisation, clearing and settlement to card transactions (Dee Hock — In memoriam). The system relied on static rules to prevent fraudulent transactions.

Most of rules-based systems were concerned with card-present fraud. They relied on velocity checks, geo anomalies and BIN blocklists.

Rules shined when it came to explainability: they were easy to understand and audit. They were perfect to work with regulators.

Rules-based approach worked well in 90s and 2000s. But fraudsters were constantly adapting their tactics to overcome new security measures. Static rules, meanwhile, were too rigid to catch new fraud schemes. The rules couldn’t automatically find and update them to reflect increasingly complex attacks caused another problem.

Another hurdle was to constantly update various thresholds to maintain acceptable rates of false positives. They weren’t as big of a problem back then, but something worth considering nevertheless.

In order to catch up with fraud schemes, rule sets had become extremely complex and hard to maintain. In its Rules based vs machine learning in fraud prevention report, PayPal says that a rule-based system may work for small companies but it’s becoming too unwieldy when it grows beyond a certain point.

To deal with the evolving fraud tactics and get around the limitations of static rules, companies turned to Machine Learning techniques.

Move to Machine Learning

Visa deployed a neural network-based AI for transaction scoring in 1993 (Visa Prevents Approximately $25 Billion in Fraud Using Artificial Intelligence). It was only a reference indicator for its clients at that time. But it wasn’t until 2010s that machine learning models got wide adoption.

By that time, companies had accumulated high volumes of labelled data. Significant advances in neural architectures and gradient-boosted tree algorithms allowed companies to use that data to deploy machine learning systems in their pipelines. They supplemented the old rules-based algorithms and increasingly handled tasks that static rules struggled with.

Mastercard launched its Decision Intelligence platform in 2016. It analyses each transaction and checks it against the cardholder’s past behaviour. Apart from solving the problem of high maintenance cost of the static rules approach, the new platform allowed Mastercard and issuers to reduce false positives.

PayPal aimed at significant fraud reduction by adopting machine learning (Doing Big Things with Big Data at PayPal). They built an ensemble of deep learning and gradient boosting models. The system checked multiple parameters to score transactions: device fingerprint, account-level risk, transaction graph.

The company later reported a transaction loss rate of just 0.08% of its total payment volume, including losses from fraud (PayPal 2025 Form 10-K).

False Positive Crisis

Every fraud-prevention system has to balance two costly kinds of error: letting fraudulent transactions through and blocking legitimate ones. Most companies naturally aimed at catching as many fraudulent transactions as possible. In other words, they minimized false negatives to protect themselves from direct financial losses, operational costs and reputational damage caused by fraud.

But stricter controls naturally led to a higher number of false positives, which companies often ignored or considered acceptable. Research by Aite Group showed how expensive that trade-off could become. It projected that losses from false declines would reach $443 billion in 2021, exceeding the losses caused by fraud itself (Financial Institutions Ease Cardholder Frustration by Addressing Transaction False Declines with New Fiserv Technology).

More recent Aite-Novarica research put the average false-decline rate for US e-commerce merchants at 1.16%. With more than $960 billion in US online sales in 2021, that translated into over $11 billion in lost legitimate sales (New Experian Link).

But banks suffered from more than just financial losses. High rate of legitimate transactions being turned down caused customers to feel upset and angry. They might leave the offending companies and turn to their competitors, which led to higher churn. Or they went to complain to regulators, who asked the companies to prove that their decisions weren’t discriminatory. Either way, high false positive rate caused significant reputational damage as well as high fraud rate.

Some companies had started to work on keeping the false positive rate low long before the report was published. Mastercard’s Decision Intelligence, introduced earlier, was one example: the company reported that it cut false positives in half. With around 75 billion transactions a year, this reduction was reported to save hundreds of millions of US dollars.

Stripe also launched its Radar Engine in 2016 (A primer on machine learning for fraud detection). They took another approach and concentrated on the merchant. Stripe calculates an acceptable level of risk for each merchant and score transactions based on that level.

For example, a B2B or enterprise software company could tolerate some losses from individual transactions to keep its reputation for high-figure contracts. In Radar 2.0 testing in 2018, Stripe said the upgraded ML models reduced fraud by more than 25% compared with the previous models without increasing the false-positive rate.

The Explainability Problem

When large amounts of legitimate transactions were turned down and the affected people complained to regulators, they had to demand greater transparency and fairness in automated decision-making. The EU introduced GDPR in 2018 which strengthened requirements around automated decisions. In the UK, the Consumer Duty introduced in 2023 added further pressure on financial firms to demonstrate that their systems produced fair outcomes for customers.

Financial institutions were now required to explain their decisions when they turned down transactions. But it was very difficult, if possible at all, to do when the decisions were made by an ML model.

HSBC tackled this problem when it developed its Dynamic Risk Assessment platform in collaboration with Google Cloud (Harnessing the power of AI to fight financial crime). They introduced SHAP values to explain machine learning predictions by measuring how much each feature contributes to a final output, using rules from cooperative game theory. HSBC put this system into production in 2021. Two years later, Google Cloud made it available for other businesses through their Anti-Money Laundering AI.

Advances in Fraud Techniques

While companies moved to more sophisticated measures to prevent fraud, fraudsters improved their methods as well. Rapid development of generative AI allowed them to launch new kinds of attacks at scale.

One of such attacks is Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud. Fraudsters manipulate victims into authorising the payments themselves. While it had been possible to use this techniques before, advances in generative AI allowed them to automatically generate highly personalized messages.

APP fraud is the most rapidly expanding form of fraud now. UK Finance report says that this type of fraud caused losses of £460 million in the UK in 2023. The most challenging part of dealing with it is that each transaction seems completely legitimate. The victim initiates the transfer, approves it on their device, nothing suspicious. How can the financial company spot a problem?

Revolut approached this problem by adding a specialized layer to their fraud-detection system (Revolut launches AI feature to protect customers from card scams). They rolled out the system in 2024.

Revolut reported a 30% reduction in losses from investment-related card scams after introducing the feature. Separately, in October 2023 they reported a 35% reduction in APP fraud since June 2023, and its broader proprietary fraud system prevented more than £475 million of fraud in 2023 (Revolut doubles Financial Crime Headcount to Combat Rising Industry Fraud).

Move to Machine Learning

item.title: Next-gen privacy protocols: WireGuard vs OpenVPN vs Shadowsocks
item.description:
WireGuard, OpenVPN, and Shadowsocks often appear in the same privacy conversation, but they were built for different jobs. WireGuard strips VPN tunneling down to a compact modern design.

OpenVPN keeps the flexibility that made it a long-running enterprise standard. Shadowsocks approaches the problem from another direction, using an encrypted proxy architecture designed to make traffic harder to classify and block.

For IT teams, that difference matters more than a generic speed ranking. The right protocol depends on whether the priority is low overhead, compatibility, or resistance to network filtering.

WireGuard keeps the tunnel deliberately small

WireGuard became popular partly because of what it leaves out. Its original Linux implementation was designed to stay under roughly 4,000 lines of code, excluding cryptographic primitives. That is tiny compared with mature VPN stacks built around TLS libraries, multiple authentication systems, and years of backward-compatible options.

The benefit is easier review. A smaller security-sensitive codebase gives auditors less implementation logic to inspect and developers fewer moving parts to configure incorrectly. It does not guarantee that vulnerabilities will never appear, but it makes the protocol easier to reason about.

WireGuard is also intentionally opinionated about cryptography. Rather than negotiating among long lists of algorithms, it uses a fixed modern suite that includes Curve25519, ChaCha20 with Poly1305, BLAKE2s, and HKDF. 

That simplicity carries into performance. WireGuard runs over UDP, uses a short handshake, and was designed for efficient packet processing. Its ability to relearn a peer’s endpoint also makes it well suited to laptops and phones that move between Wi-Fi and cellular networks.

OpenVPN still earns its place in enterprise networks

OpenVPN is considerably more complex, but much of that complexity exists for a reason. Its TLS-based architecture supports certificates, certificate authorities, revocation, external authentication systems, TCP or UDP transport, and detailed routing policies. Administrators can fit it into infrastructure that was built long before WireGuard appeared.

A company with an established public key infrastructure may therefore value OpenVPN’s controls more than a smaller codebase.

Historically, that flexibility also came with more processing overhead. OpenVPN handled much of its data path in user space, while its TLS and crypto dependencies created a larger software surface than WireGuard’s fixed design.

That performance gap is no longer as simple as old benchmark charts suggest. OpenVPN 2.6 supports Data Channel Offload on Linux, Windows, and FreeBSD, moving packet-processing work into the kernel and improving throughput considerably. 

OpenVPN is best understood as a mature, configurable system rather than simply an older and slower WireGuard. Its extra machinery can be unnecessary for a personal VPN connection and useful for exactly the same reason in an enterprise deployment.

Shadowsocks solves a different security problem

Shadowsocks is not a conventional VPN protocol. It is an encrypted proxy originally created for networks where censorship and protocol blocking are part of the threat model. 

Instead of creating the same type of layer-3 tunnel as WireGuard, Shadowsocks forwards traffic through an encrypted proxy connection. Modern implementations commonly use authenticated encryption, while the protocol avoids many of the obvious fixed signatures associated with traditional VPN traffic.

This becomes useful when a network operator is actively looking for VPN connections rather than merely inspecting their contents. A conventional VPN may encrypt every byte perfectly and still be recognizable as VPN traffic. Firewalls can examine handshake structures, packet sizes, timing, transport behavior, and other characteristics even when they cannot read the payload.

Why obfuscation is becoming harder

Older filtering systems often relied heavily on simple protocol signatures. Modern traffic classifiers can work with behavior as well.

That creates an interesting problem for Shadowsocks. Traffic that looks like high-entropy random data can defeat basic signature matching, but on an aggressively monitored network, “unrecognized encrypted traffic” can itself become something worth flagging.

Published research (PDF) has shown that Shadowsocks deployments can be detected through a mixture of passive traffic analysis and active probing. OpenVPN has faced similar research, with classifiers identifying characteristic packet patterns even when the content itself remained encrypted. 

WireGuard vs OpenVPN vs Shadowsocks

The architectural differences become clearer when the three are compared by purpose rather than by marketing labels.

This is also why having multiple protocol options in one client can be useful. Toggle says its VPN client supports WireGuard and Shadowsocks, allowing users to choose between them based on connection conditions. These product claims were not independently tested for this article.

That does not mean every connection should layer both technologies or that one automatically fixes the weaknesses of the other. The useful part is having access to different approaches without rebuilding the networking setup from scratch.

Choosing a protocol by the problem in front of you

Protocol selection gets easier when it starts with the environment instead of a favorite benchmark.

  1. Choose WireGuard when efficiency is the priority. It is a strong fit for mobile devices, remote workers, gaming, and other situations where low overhead and quick reconnection matter.
  2. Keep OpenVPN where compatibility matters more. Existing certificate systems, TCP requirements, complex routing, and older enterprise infrastructure may justify the extra complexity.
  3. Use Shadowsocks when filtering is the main obstacle. Its proxy architecture is designed for networks where recognizable VPN traffic may be restricted.
  4. Test the actual route. Server distance, packet loss, firewall policy, and local filtering can matter more than theoretical protocol performance.
  5. Do not equate encryption with invisibility. A tunnel can protect packet contents while remaining easy for a network classifier to identify.

The best protocol depends on what the network is fighting

WireGuard changed VPN design by proving that a secure tunnel could be built with far less code and far fewer configuration choices. OpenVPN remains relevant because enterprise networks often need exactly the controls WireGuard intentionally avoids. Shadowsocks tackles another problem entirely: keeping an encrypted connection usable when the network itself is trying to identify and restrict it.

For IT professionals, there is no need to force those designs into a single winner.

WireGuard is the stronger default when speed, mobility, and a small attack surface lead the requirements. OpenVPN remains useful when authentication and compatibility dominate. Shadowsocks becomes valuable when detection and blocking are part of the network environment.

(Photo by Kevin Paster)

item.title: Transferring Unused IPv4 Addresses in Asia Pacific: The Complete APNIC Playbook
item.description:
If your network needs more IPv4 space in the Asia Pacific region, the transfer market is now the main way to get it.  Asia Pacific Network Information Centre (APNIC) became the first regional registry to run out of freely allocated IPv4 on 15 April 2011, according to the IPv4 address exhaustion record.

That makes APNIC’s transfer policy the rulebook for almost every new block in the region. APNIC’s own summary page lists the permitted transfer scenarios and little else.  This guide covers the rest: who qualifies, what the registry checks, how the workflow runs, what it costs and where deals tend to stall.

Key Takeaways

  1. Both sides of a transfer inside the APNIC region must be current APNIC account holders, and the smallest block you can transfer is a /24.
  2. Buyers must show a detailed plan to use the space within 24 months. Buyers who already hold IPv4 must also show past usage and compliance with APNIC policy.
  3. Addresses delegated from APNIC’s 103/8 free pool cannot be transferred for at least five years after the original delegation.
  4. The seller starts the transfer in MyAPNIC and the buyer has 30 days to acknowledge it, or the request is cancelled.
  5. Pre-approval lets a buyer clear the needs assessment before finding a seller.
  6. The recipient generally pays APNIC’s transfer fee before the Whois record is updated.

Why APNIC Allows IPv4 Transfers

The goal of the policy is simple. It moves IPv4 from organizations that no longer need it to organizations that do but can’t get it from the free pool, as set out in the APNIC Internet Number Resource Policies.

APNIC treats addresses as licensed for use rather than owned. So a transfer is really a change in who the registry recognizes as the holder, recorded in the APNIC Whois Database.  APNIC does not recognize transfers made outside its policy and can require those addresses to be returned.

The Five Transfer Scenarios

APNIC permits five transfer paths for unused IPv4 addresses and AS numbers. Some economies in the region run their own National Internet Registry (NIR) under APNIC, which is why several paths involve one.

The scenario changes who you deal with, not the core test. Each one still asks whether the seller is the rightful holder and whether the buyer can justify the space.

What APNIC Requires From the Buyer

The recipient must be a current APNIC account holder before anything can move. From there, the test depends on whether you already hold IPv4.

A first-time holder must show a detailed plan for using the transferred space within 24 months.  An existing holder needs that plan too, plus its past usage rate and evidence that it complied with APNIC policy on earlier delegations.

The plan has to be backed by real documents. APNIC’s general request rules say evidence can include network engineering plans, subnetting plans, topology and routing descriptions, equipment invoices and purchase orders. Estimates must be realistic and justifiable, and incomplete requests wait until the gaps are fixed.

What APNIC Requires From the Seller

The source must be the currently registered holder of the block and cannot be involved in any dispute over it. The space must sit in the range APNIC administers and be allocated or assigned to a current account holder.

Three limits catch sellers most often:

  • Minimum size. Nothing smaller than a /24 can be transferred.
  • The 103/8 lock. Space delegated from APNIC’s final 103/8 pool cannot move for at least five years after the original delegation. If the original reason for the request no longer applies during that time, the addresses go back to APNIC.
  • Loss of rights. Once the transfer completes, the seller has no further rights to the addresses, according to the APNIC Transfer Conditions.

If you are buying, check the delegation date of any 103/8 block before you sign anything. A block still inside its five-year window cannot be transferred at all.

How a Transfer Runs in MyAPNIC

Every in-region transfer is lodged through MyAPNIC, APNIC’s member portal. The sequence below follows APNIC’s IPv4 Transfer Guide.

  1. Get pre-approved (optional but smart). The buyer submits the Transfer Pre-approval form in MyAPNIC before finding a source. Once approved, any transfer within the approved size moves ahead without the buyer justifying need again.
  2. The seller initiates. The source account starts the transfer in MyAPNIC and selects the addresses to move.
  3. The buyer acknowledges. The recipient has 30 days to accept the transfer. Miss that window and the request is cancelled.
  4. APNIC evaluates. The registry checks the transfer against its IPv4 transfer criteria.
  5. Fees are paid and Whois updates. The recipient pays the transfer fee, then APNIC updates the registration in its Whois Database.

Pre-approval is the step most buyers underuse. Doing it first means the needs review is settled before money changes hands, so a signed deal is far less likely to stall.

Working With a Registered Broker

Most buyers don’t have a seller lined up, which is where brokers come in. APNIC keeps a page of registered IPv4 brokers that have signed an agreement to follow its broker guidelines, including acting in good faith with both sides. 

APNIC is clear that these brokers are not its agents and that it does not endorse their services. IPv4 Connect appears on that list under its operator, Brander Group. Its marketplace sells blocks at fixed prices instead of through auctions and includes a free blacklist report with every subnet.
